content.14.3 Informed consent: Informed consent should include components listed in supplementary materials. It is an opportunity to educate patients about the proposed procedure, associated risks and benefits, and available alternatives. Assessment of patient understanding (eg, teach-back technique) should be considered. Informed consent is an ethical and legal obligation required before any invasive procedure; information should be provided simply and clearly. For emergency invasive angiography a shortened informed consent process may be appropriate, but contact with patient/family after intervention is important when patient is stable or following death. Further information in supplementary data online.
content.14.4 Research participation and consent: With unstable ACS patients it can be challenging to obtain consent for emergency procedures and to enrol in clinical trials due to need for prompt care, pain/stress, and impaired consciousness. When clinical trials are conducted, patient involvement in enrolment decisions is paramount if possible. A short witnessed verbal consent followed by written consent after the acute phase may be less stressful and better received than written consent in the acute setting. Research and consent processes must follow ethical and legal requirements of the relevant country. Further information in supplementary data online.
content.14.5 Patient satisfaction and expectatio: Focusing healthcare on patient needs/preferences can improve clinical outcomes, quality of care, and satisfaction while decreasing costs and disparities. Patient perception of care is built on interpersonal interactions, quality of clinical communication, delivery of care, and administrative management. ACS patient expectations are summarized in a figure and supplementary materials are available.
